title: Working With Financial Opinion Providers: Best Practices for M&A Attorneys
summary: Learn how M&A counsel can strengthen fairness and solvency opinion engagements through better timing, diligence, projections and board oversight.
body_markdown:
In providing[fairness and solvency opinions](https://www.cbiz.com/services/advisory/valuation/financial-opinions) in complex transactions, the quality of the opinion usually reflects the quality of the process around it. Sound valuation analysis is essential, but timing, scope, information flow, and the board’s engagement matter just as much.


The role of a financial opinion is to help directors evaluate the financial terms and understand the judgments supporting the conclusion. Counsel plays a central role in making that process work.


## Engage the Provider Before the Timetable Becomes Compressed


To avoid last-minute issues, engage the opinion provider before the principal terms are set and the board meeting is scheduled. Early involvement does not require the provider to participate in negotiations. It simply creates room for diligence, management discussions, analytical review, the provider’s internal approval process, and a substantive board presentation. Counsel should also identify early whether an update or bring-down may be needed before closing.


## Define Precisely What the Opinion Will Address


The engagement letter should clearly identify the transaction, consideration, covered holders, addressees, opinion standard, effective date, and expected deliverables. Independence, conflicts, indemnification, reliance, disclosure, and update obligations should also be resolved at the outset.


## Treat Projections as a Record That Must Be Explained


Management projections are often the most consequential and most contestable input in a fairness analysis. Counsel should understand who prepared and approved them, why they were created, and whether they reflect the company’s ordinary planning process.


The selected case should be compared with budgets, prior forecasts, lender cases, and board materials. Differences are not necessarily a problem, but they should be understood. The record should explain why a particular forecast was selected and, if it changed, what changed, why, and how the revision affected the analysis.


From a valuation perspective, a mathematically precise discounted cash flow (DCF) does not cure an unsupported forecast. The credibility of the analysis begins with the credibility of the underlying assumptions.


## Make Sure The Analysis Reflects the Actual Transaction Economics


The headline purchase price rarely tells the whole story. Earnouts, rollover equity, seller notes, escrows, indemnities, assumed liabilities, and tax attributes can materially affect what sellers receive or retain. Counsel is usually best positioned to explain those legal mechanics to the valuation team in a fairness opinion.


This matters most when consideration depends on future performance or includes securities that are not equivalent to cash at closing. A short discussion of the operative terms can prevent the provider from analyzing an economic package that differs from the one the board is actually considering.


For a solvency opinion, the information set is broader and typically includes the legal-entity and guarantor structure, sources and uses, debt maturities, covenants, liquidity, downside scenarios, and contingent or off-balance-sheet liabilities.


## Establish a Protocol for Changes


M&A attorneys know that various transaction details can change after the initial analysis. Counsel and the provider should agree in advance on which developments must be communicated and who will determine whether updated analysis, another board discussion, or a bring-down is required.


If valuation ranges change, the reason should be documented. A simple analytical change log can help keep the board materials, opinion analysis, and transaction record aligned as the deal evolves.


## Present the Analysis, Not Only the Conclusion


The opinion letter is intentionally concise. The board presentation is where directors should see the methods, key assumptions, valuation ranges, sensitivities, and limitations supporting the conclusion.


Counsel should preserve enough agenda time for questions. If the analysis depends heavily on one method or is particularly sensitive to a forecast assumption or discount rate, for example, the board should understand that. Minutes should capture the principal analyses reviewed, material sensitivities discussed, relevant conflict diligence, and the board’s questions without becoming a transcript.


## Keep the Transaction Record Consistent


Before signing or disclosure, compare the opinion materials, management presentations, board minutes, and transaction documents. Forecast periods, valuation ranges, fees, transaction terms, and descriptions of the provider’s role should tell the same story.


Public disclosure should accurately describe the methodologies, material assumptions and inputs, valuation ranges, fees, conflicts, scope, addressees, date, and limitations of the opinion. It should not imply that financial fairness is a determination of legal fairness, fiduciary compliance, tax consequences, or transaction advisability.


## Building a Process the Board Can Stand Behind


The strength of an opinion engagement is measured by whether directors received a clear, independent financial analysis, had a meaningful opportunity to question it, and created a record that accurately reflects their process — not how quickly it was delivered. When counsel and the opinion provider work toward those objectives from the outset, the opinion can become a useful part of board decision-making rather than just another closing item.


#### Frequently Asked Questions


Engage early enough to allow for diligence, management access, analytical review, internal approval, board discussion, and any required update before closing.


The letter should cover the transaction, consideration, covered holders, addressees, opinion standard, effective date, deliverables, independence, conflicts, indemnification, disclosure, and expectations for updates or bring-downs.


Determine who prepared and approved them, why they were created, how they compare with other internal cases, and why the selected case is appropriate for the assignment.


Material changes in transaction terms, company performance, financing, capital structure, or other relevant circumstances may require updated analysis. The protocol should be established before those changes occur.
